ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Jaundice during therapy

A 16-year-old develops dark urine, jaundice and right upper quadrant discomfort 7 weeks after beginning atomoxetine. Aminotransferases are markedly elevated. Viral hepatitis testing is negative and he denies supplements or excess acetaminophen. Which medication action is most appropriate while the liver injury is evaluated?

  1. Continue at the same dose until jaundice resolves
  2. Double the dose to overcome reduced hepatic clearance
  3. Restart immediately after one normal liver test
  4. Treat the urine color as a harmless expected dye effect
  5. Discontinue atomoxetine and avoid restarting it when liver injury is attributed to it
Answer and explanation

Discontinue atomoxetine and avoid restarting it when liver injury is attributed to it

Atomoxetine has a rare serious hepatic-injury warning; jaundice with biochemical injury requires withdrawal and assessment.

Option explanations

Discontinue atomoxetine and avoid restarting it when liver injury is attributed to it: Atomoxetine has a rare serious hepatic-injury warning; jaundice with biochemical injury requires withdrawal and assessment.

Continue at the same dose until jaundice resolves: Continuing a suspected hepatotoxic exposure may worsen injury.

Double the dose to overcome reduced hepatic clearance: Reduced clearance would increase exposure rather than justify escalation.

Restart immediately after one normal liver test: Rechallenge after attributed liver injury is not recommended.

Treat the urine color as a harmless expected dye effect: Associated jaundice and elevated aminotransferases indicate a pathologic process.
